name: C5 LowKey - Flipper Zero
firmware_note: Marauder is the same open-source Wi-Fi/BLE offensive firmware that runs on dozens of bare ESP32 boards; this product is Marauder preloaded on an ESP32-C5 soldered to a Flipper GPIO breakout with GPS and a case.
price_note: Confirmed at $44.00 direct from the vendor's storefront data; all purchasable variants currently show unavailable (sold out).
skill_note: Plugs straight into Flipper GPIO and is controlled from the Flipper Marauder app, but interpreting Wi-Fi 6/5GHz scan results and wardriving logs assumes some existing Wi-Fi security background.
build_note: ESP32-C5 is soldered to the board at the factory; no user soldering. Just seat it on the Flipper's GPIO header.
summary: A Flipper Zero GPIO daughterboard with an ESP32-C5 soldered directly to the PCB (no separate DevKit needed), preloaded with ESP32 Marauder firmware. The headline feature over older ESP32-S3 Marauder boards is 5GHz Wi-Fi support, plus an onboard GPS module for wardriving logged straight to microSD.
honest_take: The silicon underneath is a $15 Espressif dev-board chip running the same open-source Marauder firmware available free for a dozen other ESP32 boards - the $44 buys assembly, the GPS module, and a case, not novel capability. The real reason to pick this over an ESP32-S3 Marauder board is genuine 5GHz support, but ESP32-C5 has a single RF front end shared between 2.4 and 5GHz - it cannot monitor or scan both bands simultaneously, only switch between them, despite 'dual-band' branding implying otherwise. It is currently sold out at the vendor.
best_for: Wardriving with GPS logging on a Flipper you already own
5GHz Wi-Fi network scanning that older Flipper Wi-Fi boards can't do
not_for: Simultaneous 2.4GHz + 5GHz monitoring
Bluetooth/BLE work (no confirmed BLE support in this firmware build)
Anyone who wants the cheapest path to the same capability (see Marauder C5 Adapter)

Onboard GPS module with ceramic patch antenna; exact GPS chip not disclosed by the vendor listing.

summary: A pre-soldered companion radio board for the HaleHound project that plugs into an ESP32 'Cheap Yellow Display' (CYD) build, combining a CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver and an NRF24L01 2.4GHz radio with wiring harnesses included. name: Sneak32
firmware_note: No stock/official variant exists - this is the only version, flashed onto a generic ESP32 board.
price_note: No official hardware is sold. This is open-source firmware you flash onto a generic ESP32-C3 board (e.g. a Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 or similar, roughly $5).
skill_note: Requires PlatformIO/Arduino toolchain setup and flashing a bare dev board yourself; no vendor support or pre-built binaries distribution described in the repo beyond source.
build_note: Flash onto a supported ESP32 board via PlatformIO; no soldering. Antenna choice (ceramic chip vs external) materially affects range.
summary: Open-source firmware for a generic ESP32 board that scans Wi-Fi beacons/probes and BLE advertisements, then flags devices that keep reappearing near the user over time as possible trackers or physical followers. A single-developer counter-surveillance project, not a commercial product.
honest_take: This is early-stage, single-maintainer firmware - version 0.0.1, 27 GitHub stars, and no commits in roughly a year as of this writing - so treat it as a proof of concept rather than dependable anti-stalking gear. Its 'detection' is exactly what any Wi-Fi/BLE scanner does: log MAC addresses, track RSSI and how many times/how recently each one was seen, and flag repeat offenders - it has no special sauce for identifying AirTags or professional trackers specifically. There's no assembled product to buy, and the range depends heavily on which antenna your chosen ESP32 board has, which the project explicitly flags as a limitation.
best_for: Hobbyists who want to understand BLE/Wi-Fi proximity-tracking detection from source
A cheap DIY starting point for a counter-surveillance scanner project
not_for: Anyone wanting a maintained, supported product
Reliable protection against a determined or well-resourced follower - this is a hobby project, not a security-tested tool

name: Hydra-ESP
firmware_note: Independently built on top of risinek's esp32-wifi-penetration-tool (Wi-Fi side) and the EvilAppleJuice project (BLE spam side) - not a fork of ESP32 Marauder, despite covering similar ground. Repo was renamed from ESP32-Deauther/HydraESP.
price_note: No official hardware. Runs on a generic ESP32 DevKit V1 (~$5-8); an optional SSD1306 128x64 I2C OLED (~$2) adds a status display.
skill_note: Flashing is straightforward, but running deauth/evil-twin/credential-harvesting attacks responsibly and legally requires understanding what you're actually doing to a network.
build_note: Flash onto a plain ESP32 (Xtensa LX6 dual-core) DevKit; optional OLED wired over I2C for status. Not compatible with ESP32-S2/S3/C3.
summary: Open-source Wi-Fi and BLE offensive firmware for a bare ESP32 board: multi-target deauthentication, WPA handshake/PMKID capture, evil-twin captive portals, BSSID cloning, a deauth detector, and Apple/Samsung/Google-style BLE advertisement spam plus BLE HID keystroke injection, all driven from a web UI at 192.168.4.1.
honest_take: Despite the project's earlier name (ESP32-Deauther/HydraESP) and feature overlap, this is not a Marauder fork - it's built on risinek's esp32-wifi-penetration-tool for the Wi-Fi attacks and the EvilAppleJuice project for BLE spam, so it has a different codebase, app ecosystem, and hardware-support list than Marauder. It only runs on the original Xtensa ESP32 (not the newer, more commonly available S2/S3/C3 boards), which is a real compatibility trap for anyone who already owns a modern ESP32 dev board. The feature list (16 simultaneous deauth targets, PMKID capture, evil twin, BSSID cloning to defeat Management Frame Protection, BLE HID payloads to Windows) is genuinely capable for a $6 board, and the project is actively maintained (203 stars, pushed within the last two months), but this is unsigned firmware doing credential harvesting and unauthorized-access-adjacent attacks - using it against networks you don't control and have authorization to test is illegal in most places, web UI polish notwithstanding.
best_for: Learning Wi-Fi/BLE attack techniques on your own test network
Authorized Wi-Fi security assessments needing a cheap, capable deauth/evil-twin platform

honest_take: This is not an SDR and cannot receive, demodulate, or capture arbitrary signals - it measures how a passive RF network (almost always an antenna) reflects and passes energy at swept frequencies, which is a completely different function that only looks superficially similar to spectrum/signal tools because of the touchscreen and SMA connectors. summary: A small, USB-powered, driver-free RF signal generator built around an Analog Devices ADF4351 synthesizer and a Microchip PIC16 controller, producing an output tone anywhere from 35MHz to 4.4GHz in 10kHz steps, with adjustable amplitude and programmable frequency sweep/hop. It is a transmit-only signal source with no receive capability.
honest_take: This is purely a test/signal source, not a transceiver - it has no receiver, no demodulation, and no ability to interact with an existing protocol beyond emitting a raw carrier at a chosen frequency. Despite being marketed as 'open source,' the license is Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives (CC BY-NC-ND), which blocks commercial use and modification/redistribution of derivative designs - meaningfully more restrictive than a typical open-hardware license (e.g. CERN-OHL or MIT), so don't assume you can freely build on or resell derivatives of this design. Output amplitude is modest (roughly -1dBm to +4dBm depending on frequency) and unfiltered straight off the synthesizer, so harmonic/spurious content should be assumed present unless you add your own filtering - treat it as a lab signal source, not a clean RF reference.
best_for: Bench-testing a receiver's sensitivity or filter response at a known frequency
Generating a reference tone across a wide 35MHz-4.4GHz range from a single cheap USB device
not_for: Any use requiring reception - it has zero RX capability
Commercial products or redistributed derivative designs - blocked by the CC BY-NC-ND license
Clean/filtered RF output - raw synthesizer output, no stated output filtering

legal.notes: Owning a signal generator is legal. summary: An expansion board for the ClockworkPi uConsole handheld Linux computer that adds an RTL2832U+R860-based RTL-SDR receiver (100kHz-1.74GHz, with HF direct sampling down to 100kHz-28.8MHz), a Semtech SX1262 LoRa radio (860-960MHz, up to 22dBm), GPS/GNSS, an RTC, and USB 3.0/Gigabit Ethernet ports, turning the uConsole into a field SDR/LoRa/wardriving platform.
honest_take: The RTL-SDR portion is receive-only - it's the same RTL2832U+R860 tuner combination found in $25 RTL-SDR dongles, just integrated onto a board with everything else; buying this specifically for wideband transmit capability would be a mistake, that job belongs to the SX1262 LoRa radio (which is TX+RX but only in the 860-960MHz LoRa band, not general-purpose). The 'USB 3.0 and RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet' headline claim comes with a real asterisk the listing itself states: full USB 3.0 and RJ45 only work with the uConsole's CM5 upgrade kit, not the base CM4 unit most existing uConsoles ship with - check which compute module you have before assuming you'll get those speeds/ports.

Wardriving/signal-hunting trips where a laptop is overkill
not_for: Anyone without a uConsole already - this is an expansion board, not a standalone product
